raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old male with no previous comorbidities presented with diffuse myalgia, headaches, retro-orbital pain and fever. On the first day of symptoms, he sought medical attention at the Dr. Serafim de Carvalho Clinical Hospital, in Jatai city, Goias State, Brazil. After performing laboratory exams and receiving intravenous hydration, the patient was sent to home care.
On the fourth day, the patient developed a respiratory-dependent chest pain despite having improved from the systemic symptoms and fever. He has also complained of a continuous abdominal pain. Edema of the lower limbs with purpuric lesions on the extremities appeared at this time (Figure 1).
The patient presented no signs or symptoms such as oral ulcers, other extremity cutaneous rashes, arthralgia, arthritis or visual acuity impairment. The laboratory blood count exam results revealed thrombocytopenia (105,000/mm3), which led to a possible dengue diagnosis. Within 48 h of hospital admission, the patient developed dyspnea and the emergence of a pericardial friction. A transthoracic echocardiography was performed, showing significant pericardial effusion, along with signs of cardiac tamponade.
The patient underwent pericardial drainage that removed 200 mL of a yellowish liquid. New laboratory exams indicated a worsening of the thrombocytopenia (80,000/mm3, urea 43 mg/dL, creatinine 1.10 mg/dL, a urinalysis showed no changes in urinary sediment, aspartate aminotransferase 97 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 69 U/L.
A chest computerized tomography (CT) showed a diffuse ground-glass image and signs of pulmonary congestion (Figure 2). Empirically, antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone and oxacillin was started for a possible bacterial infection along with prednisone 80 mg (1 mg/kg). In addition, blood cultures, antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody (ANCA), CH100, serology for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B, C, and HIV, as well as biopsy of the cutaneous lesions.
Forty-eight hours after the drain passage, the patient experienced clinical improvement, and clear pericardial fluid along with the pericardial drain were removed. The analysis of the pericardial fluid showed a citrus-yellow color fluid with exudative pattern, negative BAAR test , red cells 4,100/mm3, leukocytes 8,100/mm3 (lymphocytes 18%, neutrophils 82%), glucose 14 mg/dL, amylase 19 U/L, proteins 4.42 g/dL, in addition to negative bacterial cultures.
This treatment has also improved the patient's platelet count, attenuating symptoms 10 days after their onset. As the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and the detection of the virus nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) were not available, IgM and IgG tests for dengue were performed by an immunochromatographic method on the seventh day. The results were non-reactive for both, IgM and IgG antibodies. Later, on the tenth day, the test was repeated and this time the results were positive for both, IgM and IgG.
The cutaneous histopathological analysis was compatible with leukocytoclastic vasculitis (Figure 3). Furthermore, ANA, ANCA, hepatitis B, C, HIV, blood cultures and the serum complement were normal. The serology for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr was negative for IgM, but positive for IgG. Cutaneous lesions regressed and the patient was followed-up for six months by a nursing team (Figure 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male presenting with diffuse myalgia, headache, retro-orbital pain, and fever for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 24-year-old male presented with fever, diffuse myalgia, headache, and retro-orbital pain. After initial supportive care, systemic fever improved; however, on the fourth day, he developed respiratory-dependent chest pain, persistent abdominal pain, and bilateral lower extremity edema with purpura. Within 48 hours of inpatient admission, he developed progressive dyspnea and signs of pericardial tamponade requiring urgent pericardiocentesis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Continuous abdominal pain, lower extremity edema, purpuric lesions on extremities; absence of oral ulcers, other cutaneous rashes, arthralgias, arthritis, or visual changes.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Respiratory-dependent chest pain, dyspnea, audible pericardial friction rub; lower limb edema with purpuric lesions on the extremities; no oral ulcers or peripheral arthritis.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood count: Initial platelets 105,000/mm3, worsening to 80,000/mm3 at tamponade onset; urea 43 mg/dL, creatinine 1.10 mg/dL, AST 97 U/L, ALT 69 U/L; normal urinalysis sediment. Transthoracic echocardiography: Significant pericardial effusion with signs of cardiac tamponade. Pericardial fluid analysis (200 mL citrus-yellow exudate): Red cells 4,100/mm3, leukocytes 8,100/mm3 (82% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes), glucose 14 mg/dL, amylase 19 U/L, total protein 4.42 g/dL; negative BAAR stain and sterile bacterial cultures. Serologies: Blood cultures, ANA, ANCA, CH100, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV negative; CMV and EBV showed negative IgM with positive IgG.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Diffuse ground-glass opacities and signs of pulmonary congestion. Pericardiocentesis: Evacuation of 200 mL pericardial effusion. Skin biopsy: Cutaneous histopathological analysis compatible with leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection complicated by severe acute pericarditis with cardiac tamponade and cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Confirmatory testing showed negative IgM and IgG on day 7, with seroconversion to positive Dengue IgM and IgG by immunochromatography on day 10. Autoimmune vasculitides (ANA, ANCA, complement), acute viral hepatitides, HIV, CMV/EBV acute infection, and bacterial/tubercular pericarditis were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Emergency pericardiocentesis with drain placement (draining 200 mL) resulting in immediate hemodynamic stabilization; drain removed after 48 hours upon resolution of fluid output. Empiric IV antibiotic coverage with ceftriaxone and oxacillin, alongside oral prednisone 80 mg (1 mg/kg/day). Platelet counts normalized, dyspnea and purpuric lesions regressed, and he was discharged with uneventful 6-month clinical follow-up.
